newsitem.title: USA: Wireless PCS industry expected to grow fast.
newsitem.headline: Wireless PCS industry expected to grow fast.

text.p: The personal communications services industry expects to have more subscribers than the cellular industry by 1998, its trade group said.
But the Personal Communications Industry Association based its projection on some early starters.

Srint Spectrum L.P. and BellSouth Mobility unit of BellSouth Corp have been offering PCS service. After only 10 months of operation, Sprint Spectrum has more than 100,000 customers. "We predict by 1998 a cross over in
which there will be more digital customers than analog," said the PCIA's president Jay Kitchen. Cellular systems are primarily analog.

Sprint Spectrum is a PCS venture jointly owned by Sprint Corp, Tele-Communications Inc, Comcast Corp and Cox Communications. It announced at $600 million deal with Samsung Electronics Co Ltd for Samsung handsets.

The PCIA, which is holding a conference here this week, estimates that by 1998, half of new subscribers that year signing up for any type of wireless service will be signing up for PCS. This year only 2 percent of new wireless subscribers are signing up for PCS.

Most personal communications service (PSC) providers are just launching their businesses or currently building networks to offer service, having won spectrum for this new type of wireless service only last year in a U.S. government auction.

However, because cellular, paging and all kinds of wireless communications have been hugely successful - growing as a group about 40 percent a year, the accleration of PCS into the market won't cut off cellular's growth, the PCIA believes.

Rather, with penetration of all wireless services at only 16.6 percent of the U.S. population, there is a vast untapped market. The PCIA expects 33 percent of the U.S. population to use wireless devices in four years from now, Kitchen said.

Moreover, in the rest of the world, the wireless market is even more fertile because many developing and semi-developed countries are upgrading their telecommunications systems with wireless systems rather than build wireline infrastructures.
Nonetheless, PCS companies in the U.S. have several hurdles to overcome to do business, steming from the newness of the industry.

As PCS companies build out networks another stumbling block they've faced is municipal zoning boards who don't want wireless transmission towers in certain areas, such as residential, largely because of health risks associated with radio frequency tranmissions.

U.S. Federal Communications Commissioner Rochelle Chong said the FCC is drafting national emission standards for the PCS and cellular industry to hopefully smooth the process of getting site approvals by having a set of national environmental type standards for both municipalities and companies to go by.
